analysis.one_liner: Makes CMS publish a public list of hospitals violating the price transparency rule.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in November 2023 and referred to the Health committee, where it died without a hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals are already required by federal rule to post clear, accessible prices for their services online. This bill would force the government to publish a public list of hospitals that have been fined, warned, or told to fix noncompliance, and to make all enforcement records freely available under public records law. It would also require annual reports to Congress on enforcement and a study of stronger penalties, including potentially stripping tax-exempt status from nonprofit hospitals that don't comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and employers who need to know what care will cost before they get it. When hospitals must compete on visible prices, people can comparison shop and are less likely to be surprised by large medical bills. Self-insured employers, who pay their workers' health bills directly, would also get better data to negotiate.

how_it_helps.text: Requires CMS to maintain a public, searchable list of hospitals found out of compliance with the price transparency rule, including those fined, warned, or sent corrective-action requests.
Makes every penalty, warning notice, and enforcement communication subject to full, unredacted public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, removing the ability to keep enforcement quiet.

Requires annual reports to Congress and a government study recommending stronger enforcement, including larger fines and possible revocation of tax-exempt status for noncompliant nonprofit hospitals, followed by a formal rulemaking on those recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals that are currently posting misleading, incomplete, or no prices online would face public naming, larger penalties, and — for nonprofit hospitals — a possible threat to their tax-exempt status. Insurers and hospitals that benefit from opaque pricing lose negotiating leverage when patients and employers can see real prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals with hidden or misleading prices

drawbacks.text: Naming-and-shaming alone may not fix the problem: the existing transparency rule already carries civil monetary penalties, yet compliance has remained low, so a public list does not by itself change hospitals' behavior unless penalties grow.
The bill's toughest ideas — bigger fines and revoking nonprofit tax exemption — are only recommendations in a study, not requirements in the bill itself, so the immediate legal teeth are limited.

Hospitals argue that publishing every internal enforcement communication could be unfair to hospitals that are briefly or technically out of compliance, since even a routine warning letter would put them on a public blacklist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow but useful enforcement tool: it costs taxpayers almost nothing and mainly creates publicity pressure and paperwork discipline for hospitals that are already legally required to post prices. Its main weakness is that its strongest penalties are only recommended, not mandated, and two sponsors is far too little political weight to move it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee in November 2023, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, joined by Senator Ted Budd as its only cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that don't post their prices are better off: the existing transparency rule keeps costing them little, and no public list or stronger penalties ever took shape. Patients gained nothing because the bill never moved.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a public list of hospitals violating the price transparency rule.

for.name: Sen. Ted Budd
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the sole cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in November 2023 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans sponsored the bill and no committee or floor votes were ever held, so the partisan shape of opposition never showed up in any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would publicly name hospitals that fail to post prices, threaten bigger fines, and open the door to stripping tax-exempt status from nonprofit hospitals — direct costs to providers that profit from opaque pricing. Patients' gain from comparable prices comes out of that leverage, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

As tax-exempt charities, nonprofit hospitals get the closest look: the bill directs a study of revoking their 501(c)(3) status if they don't comply. In exchange for tax breaks, they're expected to keep care affordable, so disclosure of noncompliance serves their communities.

industries.industry: Employers that self-insure worker health plans
industries.note: Visible hospital prices give large employers real data to negotiate with providers, which flows back to workers as lower costs — the bill itself names employers as a group transparency should serve.
